Courier at the depot courtyard wall

Give the courier a feeler ahead of its travel. A hit supplies more than a warning: the surface normal tells it which way leads back into free space. Put a temporary target along that normal and let the courier pull towards it. The ray can see a wall before the courier’s body reaches it, but detection still needs time to change motion.

A courier approaches the end of a depot courtyard wall on the way to an offset delivery point. Compare its path with the same run using a ray too short to hit. The difference reveals how much of the turn comes from avoidance and how much comes from seeking the delivery.

The example in full

READ THE PSEUDOCODE

ORDINARY PSEUDOCODE

direction = normalise(velocity) if moving else lastTravelHeading
rayEnd = position + direction * rayLength
hit = intersectFiniteSegments(position, rayEnd, wallStart, wallEnd)
// Accept only intersection fractions in [0, 1]; normal opposes the ray.

if hit exists: target = hit.point + hit.normal * avoidDistance
else: target = deliveryPoint

acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(body, target)
// Seek pulls towards the selected point; it does not command a stop.

1. Cast a finite forward ray
Show this step's code
direction = normalise(velocity) if moving else lastTravelHeading
rayEnd = position + direction * rayLength
hit = intersectFiniteSegments(position, rayEnd, wallStart, wallEnd)
// Accept only intersection fractions in [0, 1]; normal opposes the ray.

Normalise the current velocity and extend it by 9; at zero speed retain the last travel heading. The local detector intersects this finite segment with the finite wall segment using cross products. Both intersection fractions must lie within the segments. It reports the actual hit point and a unit surface normal facing against the incoming ray. Parallel and collinear segments return no hit in this small detector.

2. Build a target from the hit normal
Show this step's code
if hit exists: target = hit.point + hit.normal * avoidDistance
else: target = deliveryPoint

A hit replaces the delivery point with hitPoint + normal × 6. The offset is a centre-target distance, not an automatic guarantee about the courier’s radius. The normal arrow ends at the avoidance cross. Without a hit the selected target is the delivery point, so local avoidance has no memory of the blocked route.

3. Pull with engine Seek
Show this step's code
acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(body, target)
// Seek pulls towards the selected point; it does not command a stop.

The model passes the selected target to the existing engine Seek function. It returns acceleration towards that target, capped at 8. When the target still lies ahead, a ray hit can initially leave the pull pointing towards the wall; once the courier passes the offset target the pull points back. Detection alone never sets the courier’s velocity to zero.

4. Measure body clearance and advance
Show this step's code
nearestWallPoint = (wallX, clamp(position.y, wallBottom, wallTop))
bodyClearance = distance(position, nearestWallPoint) - radius
velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
position += velocity * dt
if moving: lastTravelHeading = normalise(velocity)

Find the nearest point on the finite wall segment and subtract 1 from its distance to the courier’s centre. This body clearance stays meaningful beside the wall and round either end; a negative value means overlap. Add acceleration times 0.1 to velocity, clip speed to 4, then advance position. The local update applies no wall clamp or collision response.

Where this breaks down
When this fails, and what to reach for instead.
A longer ray is not automatically safer. Across the offered lengths from 10 to 12, the greatest body overlap in this setup is 0.74 units. These rays hit from the start and can pull towards a target still ahead before braking. A shorter ray of length 1 supplies the comparison; neither length guarantees collision-free motion.
Try the delivery straight ahead at height 0: there is no sideways cue. The courier can switch between delivery and avoidance targets while staying on the same line. A ray-based local pull does not choose a route round a wall.
A single centre ray does not sweep the whole disc. It can miss a wall edge that the courier’s radius clips. The local detector also deliberately returns no collision for parallel or collinear segments.
Several rays can alternate between adjacent faces at a corner and keep reversing the chosen target. That is the Corner trap; this straight-wall example does not implement a remedy for it.

See it elsewhere
Where public projects implement it, and the sources this study rests on.
IN PUBLIC PROJECTS
gdx-ai · RaycastObstacleAvoidance

gdx-ai’s Java steering library separates ray configurations, collision detectors and obstacle-avoidance steering.

Version 1.8.2 updates its configured rays, asks the detector for each hit and retains the nearest hit to the owner. It constructs a target using the hit normal multiplied by the owner’s bounding radius plus distanceFromBoundary, then normalises the offset to maximum acceleration. No hit produces zero steering, so another behaviour must supply travel. The source discusses corner trapping and alternative ray configurations.

Corner trap
Reach for Corner trap when adjacent faces make ray-selected targets alternate and the character cannot free itself.
Ray configurations
Ray configurations is the next choice when one centre feeler misses edges or needs side coverage in a passage.
Collision detector interface
The Collision detector interface separates geometry from steering when several obstacle shapes must provide consistent hit points and normals.
Seek
Seek is the actual motor used here once a ray hit has supplied a temporary target.
Collision avoidance
Collision avoidance predicts another moving centre’s closest approach; use it for moving characters rather than a static surface normal.
